segments.title: Wolford Chapel: a Canadian heritage site in Devon
segments.body: Wolford Chapel illustrates why historians draw attention to historical places and encourage visits. Built in 1802 on the Simcoe family estate, it commemorates John Graves Simcoe's time as the first lieutenant governor of Upper Canada. Ontario Heritage took over the chapel in 1982, and Ontario still owns it. That history makes the chapel a small piece of Canada in Devon, with links to both Canadian and British history. It also serves as a memorial to what Canadians and Britons have achieved together. The building brings the Simcoe family, Upper Canada, and later Ontario stewardship together in one place.

evidence.note: Wolford Chapel links John Graves Simcoe and Upper Canada with Ontario's continuing ownership of a Canadian-British heritage site in Devon, making it useful for historians' public outreach.

segments.summary: Wolford Chapel is a Devon chapel linked to John Graves Simcoe and Upper Canada, and Ontario now owns the site.

segments.title: Why visits help preserve historical places
segments.body: The empty visitor book makes the preservation problem concrete: no one else had recorded a visit to Wolford Chapel that day. The site is small, but it is clearly marked, accessible, and normally open, so reaching it is not the main obstacle. Historical places can be forgotten when people stop visiting or paying attention to them. Their stories and lessons can then slip from public awareness. Historians publicize sites and events, including on social media, to encourage visits. Those visits help keep both the place and its history visible and may encourage others to return.

evidence.note: The transcript uses the empty visitor book, the chapel's accessibility, and the risk of forgotten stories to explain why historians encourage visits to historical sites.

segments.summary: An empty visitor book at accessible Wolford Chapel supports the argument that attention and visits help preserve historic places and their stories.
